questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

I. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$

II. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2 + 4}$$

III. $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^n$$

options.why: Check each series with an appropriate test: I converges, II converges, III diverges.
Check each series with an appropriate test: I converges, II converges, III diverges.
Check each series with an appropriate test: I converges, II converges, III diverges.
Correct. I: converges (alternating series test, but the harmonic series diverges). II: converges (smaller than the convergent p-series with p = 2). III: diverges (geometric with |r| = 5/4 ≥ 1).

questions.explanation: Series I converges: alternating series test, but the harmonic series diverges. Series II converges: smaller than the convergent p-series with p = 2. Series III diverges: geometric with |r| = 5/4 ≥ 1.

parts.prompt: Use the data to estimate $$P'(7)$$. Show the computations and indicate units.

rubric.criterion: Sets up the trapezoidal sum with unequal widths.

rubric.example: The total number of people who enter the park during the first 12 minutes.

parts.prompt: Must there be a time $$c$$, for $$3 < c < 9$$, such that $$P'(c) = 0$$? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Answers yes, citing the Mean Value Theorem (or Rolle's Theorem) with its conditions.
rubric.example: Yes. $$P$$ is differentiable (so continuous), and $$P(3) = P(9) = 75$$. By the Mean Value Theorem there is a $$c$$ with $$P'(c) = \frac{75 - 75}{6} = 0$$.

parts.prompt: Must there be a time $$t$$, for $$0 < t < 3$$, at which $$P(t) = 61$$? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Answers yes, citing the Intermediate Value Theorem and continuity.
rubric.example: Yes. $$P$$ is continuous, and $$61$$ is between $$P(0) = 57$$ and $$P(3) = 75$$, so the IVT guarantees such a $$t$$.

parts.prompt: Find the first three nonzero terms and the general term of the Maclaurin series for $$f'(x)$$. Then write $$f'(x)$$ as a rational function.
Use the first two nonzero terms of the series to approximate $$f(1)$$. Show that this approximation differs from $$f(1)$$ by less than $$0.008$$.

rubric.criterion: Uses the alternating series error bound with justification.
rubric.example: The series at $$x = 1$$ alternates with terms decreasing to 0, so the error is at most the third term, $$\frac{1}{3\cdot 64} = \frac{1}{192}$$.
